You don't have any Lincoln International application or interview saved on file yet. The one step that starts that record is: paste the interview invite (copy of the email or calendar entry) or tell me the date, time, format (onsite / video / phone), and who you'll meet. I'll save it and build the tailored brief.

For now, quick prep for a final-round analyst interview at Lincoln International — focused, practical, and what they'll listen for.
1) What they'll want to hear (first sentence, then why)
- Technical competence: clear accounting & Excel basics (3-statement linkage, EBITDA adjustments, working-capital mechanics). They want to trust you can build and check models under time pressure.
- Deal judgment & commercial intuition: thoughtful questions about valuation multiples, what drives enterprise value in the target industry, and risks in a transaction.
- Execution & diligence habits: concrete examples showing you can run a data request, chase counterparties, and deliver clean materials on tight timelines.
- Fit and resilience: that you can work long hours, learn fast, take feedback, and be a calm teammate in stressful deals.
2) 8 likely question types and how to answer each (what to include)
- Walk me through your resume / Why investment banking / Why Lincoln?
- Structure: 60–90s. One-line present role + 2–3 deal/impact bullets (what you did, outcome, metric), then why IB (specific skills you want), then why Lincoln (beyond prestige — mention deal teams, sector focus, or culture from your research).
- Technical: "Walk me through a three-statement model" or "How does an increase in working capital affect cash?"
- Answer with step sequence and the key linkages; mention one example of when you rebuilt or fixed a model and what you changed.
- Valuation: "How do you value a company? When do you use DCF vs. comps?"
- Name the methods (DCF, comps, precedent transactions, LBO occasionally), give 1–2 strengths/weaknesses and one short rule of thumb for when each is used.
- Accounting nuance: "If a company capitalizes R&D, how does that affect EBITDA and free cash flow?"
- Say: EBITDA up (since R&D no longer expense), depreciation up later, NOPAT and FCF impacted by capex vs. expense — give the cash vs. accrual distinction.
- Deal experience behavioral: "Tell me about a time you owned a workstream on a deal."
- Use STAR: Situation (1 line), Task (1 line), Action (focus on tools, numbers, stakeholders — what you did), Result (metric or clear outcome). Lead with your action.
- Problem-solving on the spot: case or mini-analysis (read a case, ask good clarifying questions, make assumptions explicit).
- Say your clarifying questions, state assumptions numerically, show arithmetic and logic, conclude with recommendation and key sensitivities.
- Stress / teamwork: "Tell me about a time you missed a deadline or had conflict."
- Show ownership, the correction you made, what you learned; keep it brief and forward-looking.
- Culture / fit: "How do you manage long hours?" or "How will you add value as an analyst?"
- Be specific: give a concrete habit (checklists, version control, templates) and a short example of doing the grunt work that freed senior time.
3) Two practice answers (score-ready format) — use these templates and plug your facts
- Behavioral: "Tell me about a time you found an error in a model before submission."
- Template answer (2–3 lines): "On [deal/project], I was preparing the valuation model (situation). I noticed the revenue growth assumption was copied from an old case and ran a sensitivity check (action). I corrected the assumption, reran the outputs, and we avoided an overvaluation of ~15% that would have misled the client (result)."
- What interviewers listen for: you noticed it, you quantified impact, you corrected it and communicated the change.
- Technical: "Walk me through a DCF in two minutes."
- Template: "Project unlevered free cash flows for 5 years from EBIT*(1-tax) + D&A - capex - ΔWC. Discount using WACC to enterprise value. Add non-core assets, subtract net debt to get equity value, divide by shares for per-share. Use terminal value by either Gordon growth or exit multiple; sensitivity on WACC and terminal multiple drives most value. Key checks: implied exit multiples align with comps and sum of parts reconcile to precedent transactions."
- Interviewers listen for crisp sequence, awareness of checks and sensitivity.
4) Last-round specifics at a boutique like Lincoln (what to emphasize)
- Sector focus: show knowledge of one sector they cover (pick one relevant to your background). Mention two recent Lincoln deals or a sector trend and a sensible question about it.
- Client impact stories: partners care about you protecting the client and minimizing risk — stress accuracy, discretion, and responsiveness.
- Cultural fit: be personable, show curiosity, and show product ownership (volunteer to do the heavy lift, track details).
5) Quick checklist for the interview day (practical)
- Bring one printed copy of your resume and a one-page deal sheet (3 bullets per deal: your role, deliverable, outcome).
- Prepare 3 thoughtful questions: about deal flow in a sector, what makes a successful analyst there, and a current Lincoln deal detail.
- Rehearse a 90s "why Lincoln" that links your background to their sector and the team you'll join.
- Be ready to do quick arithmetic on a tablet/sheet; practice 2–3 mental math items (percent change, multiple calculations).
- Rest, hydrate, get to camera-ready if video (background, blazer, headphones).
6) One-minute mock start (I can ask this first if you want live practice)
- I'll ask: "Walk me through your resume in 90 seconds." Answer out loud here; I'll score it for structure, evidence and specificity, then give one concrete fix and the next question.

Next step (one clear action): paste the interview invite or tell me date/time/format/people OR pick the mock start now. Which do you want me to do?

What I'll include, field by field, on the prepared application card for that first posting (plain words, each field I will fill from the posting or from your confirmed facts):

1) Posting reference
- What it is: the exact posting link and the posting's reference or ID as shown on the employer board.
- Where it comes from: the posting itself.
- Why it matters: ties this card to the exact job you asked about.
2) Employer (company)
- What it is: company name exactly as the posting shows.
- Where it comes from: the posting.
- Why it matters: used on the application and in your tracker.

3) Role / Job title
- What it is: the title the employer lists.
- Where it comes from: the posting.
- Why it matters: visible to recruiter and used for matching.

4) Work location / remote status
- What it is: city, state or "Remote", plus any onsite/hybrid days required.
- Where it comes from: the posting.
- Why it matters: commute, relocation and ATS filters.
5) Pay
- What it is: exact base or range as the posting states, or "not listed" if absent.
- Where it comes from: the posting.
- Why it matters: for your decision and negotiation prep.

6) Application method
- What it is: how they accept applications (company careers page form, external board, email, LinkedIn apply, etc.).
- Where it comes from: the posting.
- Why it matters: determines the fields I prepare (file uploads, text answers).

7) Required materials
- What it is: which documents or links the employer asks for (resume, cover letter, portfolio, references, transcripts, code samples).
- Where it comes from: the posting.
- Why it matters: so the card lists attachments to provide.
8) Pre-screen / assessment steps listed
- What it is: any stated assessments, work samples, or pre-screen questions and their format.
- Where it comes from: the posting.
- Why it matters: we may need to prepare answers or schedule time.

9) Key qualifications / required skills (parsed)
- What it is: a short bullet list of must-haves the posting lists (years of experience, degrees, specific tools, certs).
- Where it comes from: the posting.
- Why it matters: shows where your confirmed facts match or leave gaps.

10) Preferred skills / nice-to-haves
- What it is: extra skills that strengthen an application.
- Where it comes from: the posting.
- Why it matters: used for tailoring.
11) Knock-out flags / risks
- What it is: statements likely to disqualify (e.g., requires US authorization, specific years, degree).
- Where it comes from: the posting.
- Why it matters: helps you decide whether to apply.

12) Tailoring notes
- What it is: specific, short instructions I will use to tailor your resume and the 2–3 sentence cover note or resume summary for this posting (phrased to match the posting).
- Where it comes from: my reading of the posting plus your confirmed facts (none on file yet; I will only use confirmed facts after you confirm them).
- Why it matters: increases ATS and recruiter match.
13) Resume version to attach
- What it is: which resume persona or base resume will be attached; if none exists or a new tailored resume is needed, the card will state that and show the tailored changes.
- Where it comes from: your confirmed facts and any saved persona.
- Why it matters: you must confirm which contact name/email and facts to include.

14) Contact info to appear on resume & application
- What it is: the name and email exactly as you want them to appear.
- Where it comes from: what you supply here (I won't guess or use account email).
- Why it matters: required; the card will ask you to set these if missing.
15) Draft short answers to application questions
- What it is: suggested text for common short-answer fields (e.g., "Why this role?", "Salary expectations", "Visa status", "Notice period").
- Where it comes from: the posting and your confirmed facts (drafts use placeholders for missing facts).
- Why it matters: these appear on the card for you to edit before sending.

16) Draft cover letter / short note (≤120 words if email)
- What it is: a tailored cover letter or short message with brackets where facts are missing.
- Where it comes from: my draft based on the posting and your confirmed facts.
- Why it matters: increases chance of being read; it stays a draft until you approve.
17) Attachments
- What it is: the resume PDF(s), portfolio links, certificates or samples to attach.
- Where it comes from: PDFs I make from your confirmed facts or links you provide.
- Why it matters: nothing is attached until you approve the card.

18) Submission metadata & tracking
- What it is: date prepared, prepared by, card status ("Prepared — awaiting your approval"), and next recommended action (e.g., "Approve to queue for sending", "Practice for screening question X").
- Where it comes from: system.
- Why it matters: shows what happens next.
19) One-click actions shown on the card
- What they are: Edit contact, Select resume persona, Edit cover note, Save draft, Queue to apply (which only queues and does not send), or Reject (skip).
- Where it comes from: system UI.
- Why it matters: you control every next move.

20) Notes & recommended prep
- What it is: any quick interviewer prompts, likely screening questions from the posting, and a 3-step prep suggestion.
- Where it comes from: the posting and my experience tailoring for similar roles.
- Why it matters: lets you prepare right after approving.
